notes.claim: Your notes say a mains-frequency HV withstand test needs very high power because of cable capacitance, and that lowering the frequency raises the capacitive reactance and cuts the power and current needed.
The power needed to energise a cable capacitance is proportional to test frequency. One source gives 500 times less energy at 0.1 Hz than at 50 Hz, another 600 times less power than at 60 Hz.
Traditional 50/60 Hz testing was impractical on site because of the strong capacitive nature of cables.
DC testing built up space charge that accelerated water tree growth in healthy XLPE. VLF reverses polarity, which reduces that build-up but is still a compromise.
IEEE 400.2 covers VLF below 1 Hz, most commonly 0.1 Hz, with recommended test voltages for installation, acceptance and maintenance.
The VLF test range is taught as contested: the notes give 1.5 to 2.5 U0, while the IEEE guide as reproduced by High Voltage Inc bases installation and acceptance levels on practice of up to 3 U0.
notes.contested: Your notes give 1.5 to 2.5 U0 for installation, acceptance and maintenance. IEEE 400.2 as reproduced by High Voltage Inc bases installation and acceptance on practice of from less than 2 U0 to 3 U0, with maintenance about 75% of acceptance.

notes.claim: U0 is the rated rms phase-to-ground voltage. IEEE 400.2 Table 3 (sinusoidal, 69 kV class) as reproduced by High Voltage Inc lists 75, 84 and 63 kV rms for installation, acceptance and maintenance.
Recommended minimum time is 60 min at 0.1 Hz for installation or acceptance on new cable, and 30 min for a simple withstand on aged cable. The notes list the same durations.

A VLF withstand test excites any defect large enough at the test voltage, which triggers partial discharge in it. Your notes add that a severe defect starts an electrical tree that grows in the insulation.
Terminations may need to be added to avoid flashover for installation tests on cables rated above 35 kV.
Long cables need a lower frequency, a lower voltage or both, but lowering the frequency needlessly is to be avoided. A pass means the voltage held for the full duration with no breakdown.
Your notes call VLF an AC hi-potential test at a lower frequency, run at 0.1 and 0.01 Hz, and end it by applying the discharge stick, then the hook, then the hand earth.
ABB lists 0.22 µF/km and 2.6 A/km at 50 Hz for a three-core 66 kV XLPE submarine cable of 240 mm².

A VLF set is rated by the load capacitance it can test at each frequency, and the lower the frequency the longer the cable it can test. A 0.75 µF set at 0.1 Hz takes twice that load at 0.05 Hz. One 200 kV peak set is listed at 0.75 µF at 0.1 Hz up to 3.75 µF at 0.02 Hz; a 120 kV peak set at 0.55 µF at 0.1 Hz.
A set should run at 0.1 Hz unless the cable is too big a load for its rating there. A full cycle at 0.1 Hz takes 10 seconds, 20 seconds at 0.05 Hz and 50 seconds at 0.02 Hz.

VLF sets are rated in kV peak, and a sine wave's rms is 0.707 of its peak. IEEE 400.2 Table 3 gives the 69 kV class installation level as 75 kV rms (106 kV peak). The largest 0.1 Hz sets reach about 200 kV peak.

The defect picture: a defect big enough to be excited by the applied voltage grows to failure during the test, and lesser defects are not affected. Time can be shortened to 15 to 30 minutes if the monitored characteristic stays stable and nothing fails, against the 60 minute recommendation.

U0 is the rated rms power frequency voltage between conductor and earth or metallic screen. In a rating such as 38/66 (72.5) kV, 38 kV is U0, 66 kV is U between conductors and 72.5 kV is the highest system voltage Um.
DC withstand testing of extruded cable has been discouraged by IEEE 400.1, ICEA S-94-649 and IEC 60502-2; DC can induce space charge in XLPE that contributes to degradation.

After any high-voltage test an XLPE cable holds charge in its capacitance and its dielectric. Residual voltage can persist for minutes or even hours and voltage can rebound after a first discharge, so discharge with a stick, apply a direct ground and keep it connected, then measure the residual voltage before anyone gets access. Test at 2 U0 or 2.5 U0 raises the stored energy, which grows with the square of the voltage.

Whether VLF suits a 66 kV inter-array cable is contested. The notes and IEEE 400.2 (a guide for cables rated 5 kV to 69 kV) support a 0.1 Hz VLF withstand; but a test-system maker reads IEC 63026 as requiring 10 to 500 Hz for commissioning cables above 36 kV, and 66 kV array strings have been commissioned with resonant AC sets per IEC 63026. CIGRE TB 490 says a lower frequency down to 10 Hz can be acceptable for long submarine cables. The IEC 63026 clause text is paywalled and was not seen.
notes.contested: Your notes and IEEE 400.2 teach a 0.1 Hz VLF withstand as the field test; a test-system maker says IEC 63026 asks for 10 to 500 Hz on cables above 36 kV, and resonant AC sets are used on 66 kV array strings. The clause itself was not seen, so the client's specification settles it.
